1.narration: Hundreds of thousands of years ago, an elephant lived on Sicily.

39.narration: He never mentions a forehead. He says 'the eye', and presumably his audience knew.

40.narration: For a plain statement, one eye in the forehead, we need a different poet.

57.narration: So that is the myth. Is there anything solid underneath it?
57.note: Standing cutout on white, ground line

59.note: Dots on Sicily, Malta, Crete, Cyprus, Tilos

61.narration: They descended from a straight-tusked elephant about four metres tall,
61.note: Same sprite scaled to 4 m. On-screen note: proportions simplified

62.note: Shot 2 asset again with a shoulder-height line

64.narration: Now look at the skull from the front.

70.narration: The idea found a champion in Adrienne Mayor, a Stanford folklorist and historian of science.
70.note: Name, book, 2000. Typography only; no cover art, no portrait

71.narration: In The First Fossil Hunters, she argues that Greeks and Romans noticed big fossil bones,
71.note: Sanctuary porch, giant bone on a plinth, two tiny visitors. DRIFT: new faces; keep them tiny

72.narration: collected them, measured them, and tried to explain them.
72.note: Crop on the bone, rod overlay

73.narration: Giants, and one-eyed monsters, may owe something to those finds.
73.note: Different crop; the word 'may' picked out

74.narration: On the Cyclops, though, Mayor herself is careful.

75.narration: She does not like to say the fossils were the source of the story,
75.note: Short quote overlay, credited to Discover Magazine

76.narration: 'because we just can't prove that.' We do not know, she says, which came first.
76.note: Two arrows: myth > bones? / bones > myth?

77.narration: Perhaps the myth came first, and the bones merely seemed to confirm it.

78.narration: Then there is a problem with the most famous version of this theory.

79.narration: Abel claimed that the philosopher Empedocles reported finding such bones on Sicily.

80.narration: Later researchers have found no surviving ancient source that says so.

81.narration: The palaeontologist Mark Witton and Richard Hing put it bluntly:

82.narration: without that story, they argue, the idea becomes baseless.

83.narration: Elephant fossils and one-eyed monsters turn up all over the world,
83.note: World outline, two labels, no site dots (not verified)

84.narration: and no ancient text or artwork makes the Sicilian link stand out.

85.narration: The scholars of Greek myth Mercedes Aguirre and Richard Buxton make a similar point.

86.narration: Theories like this sound plausible, they say,
86.note: PLAUSIBLE ticked, CHAIN OF ARGUMENT blank

87.note: Slow dissolve back to the skull; 'chain of argument' row stays blank

90.narration: Hesiod, writing around 700 BC, names three Cyclopes: Brontes, Steropes, and Arges.
90.note: BRONTES thunder / STEROPES lightning / ARGES bright

91.narration: Thunder, Lightning, and Bright. They forge the thunderbolt for Zeus.
91.note: Tongs, hammer and a thunderbolt on the anvil, sparks. No faces

92.narration: And Hesiod is the one who says it plainly:
92.note: Tight on the face, single eye

93.narration: 'one eye only was set in the midst of their foreheads.'

94.narration: These are not cannibal shepherds. They are craftsmen, working for the king of the gods.

95.narration: Same name, same eye, completely different job.

96.narration: The scholar Walter Burkert suggested the smith Cyclopes may reflect real guilds of metalworkers.

97.narration: Later poets merged the two. Virgil puts Brontes and Steropes in a forge under Etna.

98.narration: By the fifth century BC, the Cyclopes are living on Sicily.
98.note: Standing cutout against the Etna background; Stage pass with rim light from the glow

115.narration: The wall is real. The Cyclopes were the Greeks' explanation for it.

121.narration: So where does that leave us? Start with what is solid.

122.narration: The Greeks told at least three different Cyclops stories, and kept them apart.

123.narration: A single eye is stated by Hesiod, Euripides, and Theocritus. Homer implies it.
123.note: Three ticked rows; Homer row marked 'implied'

124.narration: Dwarf elephants really lived on those islands,
124.note: Skull plate with island dots inset

125.narration: and their skulls really do have a hole in the middle.
125.note: B shot: second crop or state of the same image, hard cut at the phrase break

126.narration: The blinding story itself is a folktale. Scholars have counted over two hundred versions,
126.note: Regional markers only (Iceland, Britain/Ireland, Portugal, Africa, Turkey, Russia, Arabia, Korea)

127.narration: from Iceland to Korea, and most think the tale is older than Homer.

128.narration: That does not rule out the skull.

129.narration: It does mean the story does not need one.
129.note: B shot: second crop or state of the same image, hard cut at the phrase break

131.narration: No surviving ancient text says anyone mistook a skull for a Cyclops.
131.note: B shot: second crop or state of the same image, hard cut at the phrase break

132.narration: Other explanations compete: volcanic craters, smith guilds, even a birth defect called cyclopia,

133.narration: though in that condition the eye sits below the nose, not above it.

134.narration: Aguirre and Buxton's verdict is that each has an air of plausibility,

135.note: B shot: next state of the same card

136.narration: The skull theory is a hypothesis. A plausible one, and still unproven.

139.narration: As a one-eyed giant who eats sailors, no.

140.narration: But the name covers at least four different things:

141.narration: Hesiod's thunderbolt smiths, Homer's shepherd, a volcano's worth of Sicilian tradition,
141.note: Four-panel montage, panels reveal in turn

142.narration: and walls you can still touch.

143.narration: The skull may be one more thread. It is a suspect, not a conviction.
